newsitem.title: FRANCE: RTRS-Frenchman wins incident-packed Vendee globe yacht race.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Frenchman wins incident-packed Vendee globe yacht race.

text.p: Frenchman Christophe Auguin sailed to victory on Monday in the dramatic Vendee Globe solo round-the-world-race marked by risky rescues and the disappearance of Canadian sailor Gerry Roufs.

The disaster-prone 23,112-nautical mile race made headlines after three vessels, including that of Briton Tony Bullimore, capsized in remote Antarctic seas last January, stretching the Australian Navy rescue service to the limit.

After 105 days and 20 hours alone on his 18-metre (60 ft) vessel Geodis, Auguin reached the western French resort of Les-Sables-d'Olonne at 0933 (0833 GMT), breaking the 109-day race record set in 1989 by another Frenchman, Titouan Lamazou. Dozens of yachts escorted Auguin, 37, as he crossed the finishing line for a 400,000-franc ($73,000) prize, and tens of thousands of cheering people lined the banks as he sailed slowly into port.

"This is the toughest race I have ever taken part in. The best day is today," Auguin, at a loss for words after months of solitude, said as he popped open a giant bottle of Champagne. He promptly retreated to his cabin for a half-an-hour of privacy with his wife Veronique and 18-month-old son Erwan.
His nearest rivals, Frenchmen Marc Thiercelin and Herve Laurent, were nearly 2,000 miles behind.
Auguin, who has twice previously won solo round-the-world races, said the Vendee Globe Challenge would be his last.
"I must call it a day. You feel terribly lonely at sea and this race wil mark me to the end of my life," he said.
The third Vendee Globe Challenge, in which competitors are disqualified if they touch land, has confirmed its reputation as one of the world's most dangerous sports events.
Only seven of the 16 competitors are still in the race, which skirts southern Africa and rounds Antarctica clockwise towards Cape Horn in lonely, towering seas often peppered with icebergs.
Roufs went missing over a month ago in a remote Antarctic area between New Zealand and Cape Horn in some of the world's heaviest seas.
Although all signs are that his yacht must have sunk, Auguin said hope was not lost and the Canadian may still turn up.
"We have to wait two weeks for his arrival here," he said. Bullimore and Frenchman Thierry Dubois were plucked from the sea in dramatic rescues by Australian Navy helicopters.
Bullimore spent four days trapped in his overturned yacht as an Australian frigate sped to his rescue.
Dubois' yacht sank minutes after a helicopter dropped him a life raft.
Another Frenchman, Raphael Dinelli, was rescued by British fellow competitor Pete Goss and taken to Tasmania. Goss, who was allowed to resume the race, sailed past Cape Horn last week.

Most other sailors, including France's Isabelle Autissier, who was also rescued by the Australian Navy in a previous Vendee Globe Challenge, were disqualified after port calls to fix equipment damaged in collisions with unidentified objects or marine animals.
"My old pal. I'm pleased for him," Autissier radioed Auguin from somewhere near the Canary islands.

French Prime Minister Alain Juppe wrote to Auguin saying he had performed "a major sports and human feat...I am sure your victory will give hope to all those in our society who...seek landmarks to give their life a meaning."
But the accidents and the costly rescues have triggered charges that the race was too hazardous and that yacht-builders had sacrificed safety to speed.
Critics have said the race should be abandoned or modified to ban competitors from sailing so far south.

The French Yachting Federation said it would organise a meeting of world yachting associations, competitors, Australian rescuers, weather experts, foreign race organisers, shipbuilders and navy officials in the spring to review safety problems.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
